analysis.one_liner: Strengthenes the federal guarantee for multiemployer pension plans and restricts risky pension fund practices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committee, receiving no cosponsors and no committee or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Multiemployer pension plans are retirement funds shared by groups of employers, often unions and companies in the same industry. When such plans collapse, the federal Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation backs a portion of the benefits — but the guaranteed amounts were low. This bill would raise the guaranteed benefit levels roughly doubling them, stop pension trustees from increasing benefits in poorly funded plans, require clearer disclosure of a plan's funding status, and raise the insurance premiums plans pay into the federal guarantee fund to cover the stronger benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees earning pension benefits through multiemployer pension plans, particularly those in plans that might fail; they would receive larger guaranteed benefits if their plan becomes insolvent, plus earlier warnings about a plan's financial condition.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the PBGC's guaranteed multiemployer benefit levels — for example, from $15 to $33 per month per year of service in the top category [S2][S3].

Bars trustees of asset-deficient plans (funded at 95% or less) from increasing benefits, and limits benefit increases in better-funded plans that would push funding below 90%, reducing the risk that generous promises lead to insolvency [S2][S3].
Requires plan trustees to notify participants, beneficiaries, and contributing employers each year of the plan's funded percentage and the limits of the PBGC guarantee, in plain language [S2][S3].
Standardizes interest-rate and mortality assumptions for calculating current liability and withdrawal liability, so funding problems are measured realistically [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multiemployer pension plans and their contributing employers pay higher PBGC insurance premiums ($3.50 per participant in 1999, rising to $5.20 by 2001); employers also gain a new right to sue plans to block impermissible benefit increases, which could add legal friction; and plan trustees face new restrictions on promising benefit increases that plans cannot fund.

drawbacks.text: Phased-in premium increases raise costs for the employers who fund multiemployer plans — $3.50 per participant in 1999 rising to $5.20 after 2000 [S3].
Restrictions on benefit increases constrain union-trustee decisions in weakly funded plans, potentially limiting negotiated pension improvements even before a plan is truly insolvent [S3].
Employers gain a new right to sue plans and obtain attorney's fees, which could increase litigation between employers and joint labor-management boards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades modestly higher premiums and limits on benefit promises for a substantially stronger federal guarantee and earlier warning of funding trouble. For workers facing the real risk of multiemployer plan failure, the larger guaranteed floor ($15→$33 in the top category) and mandatory funding disclosures are meaningful protections; the costs fall mainly on contributing employers, in amounts that are small relative to the insurance they buy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on November 9, 1997, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeffords introduced the Workers' Pension Protection Act on November 9, 1997 [S1][S2].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill never received a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multiemployer pension plans and contributing employers are better off because the bill died: they avoid the higher PBGC premiums and the new restrictions on benefit increases and litigation exposure. Workers in weakly funded plans did not get the stronger federal guarantee or the mandatory funding-status disclosures.

for.name: Sen. James M. Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; served as chair of the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which could have brought it up.

for.name: The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation
for.what_they_did: Would administer the larger guaranteed benefits and collect the higher premiums had the bill passed; PBGC officials had publicly urged stronger multiemployer funding rules and higher premiums during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No votes occurred and no groups formally opposed the bill on the record; it simply stalled in committee with zero cosponsors.

industries.industry: Multiemployer pension plans (jointly trusteed union plans)
industries.note: The bill would have restricted these plans' ability to increase benefits in weakly funded plans and subjected them to litigation from contributing employers, while giving participants stronger disclosures and larger PBGC guarantees.
They would pay higher PBGC premiums ($3.50–$5.20 per participant) but also gain a new right to sue plans to block unaffordable benefit increases, protecting them from unexpected withdrawal liability.
The PBGC's multiemployer program would see its costs rise (larger guaranteed benefits) alongside higher premium income, strengthening the program's finances if claims remained contained.
